Your event filled the room, but did it fill the pipeline? Leadership wants numbers, and “great energy” isn’t one. **Event marketing KPIs** turn every campaign, check-in, and conversation into data you can act on.


This guide covers 12 KPIs to track before, during, and after your event, each with a formula and a worked example. You’ll also learn how to set up attribution so you can track event marketing performance channel by channel and how InEvent captures that data automatically.

##


**What Are Event Marketing KPIs?**


Event marketing KPIs are measurable numbers that show whether your event promotion and experience met a business goal. They track how many people registered, who showed up, how engaged attendees were, and how much pipeline or revenue followed. Good KPIs tie each metric to one goal, one owner, and one deadline.


Event marketing metrics and general event KPIs overlap, but the focus differs. General event KPIs judge the event as a whole, from venue logistics and budget to the


**[25 metrics that show whether an event succeeded](https://inevent.com/blog/others/25-key-metrics-for-measuring-event-success.html)** . Event marketing KPIs zoom in on the marketing side: which channels drove sign-ups, what each attendee cost, and what revenue the event influenced.


##


**How Do You Choose the Right Event Marketing KPIs?**


Choose event marketing KPIs by starting with the goal, not the metric. Write down the one business outcome the event must deliver, such as pipeline, brand awareness, or customer retention. Then pick two to four KPIs that prove that outcome, set a target for each, and agree on where the data will come from before launch.


Event goal KPIs that prove it


**Generate pipeline** Leads and marketing qualified leads, pipeline influenced, event marketing ROI


**Reach new audiences** Registrations by channel, registration conversion rate, cost per registration


**Build brand awareness** Social reach, branded hashtag use, email open rate


**Deliver value to customers** Attendance rate, session attendance, net promoter score


**Prove profitability** Cost per attendee, event marketing ROI


InEvent event strategists recommend capping each event at five KPIs. With more than five, nobody owns the follow-up, and the report turns into a data dump instead of a decision.


##


**12 Event Marketing KPIs to Track Before, During, and After Your Event**


KPIs 1–4 tell you whether your promotion is working while there’s still time to fix it. KPIs 5–7 show what happens on the day. KPIs 8–12 prove the business result. Formulas and worked examples for each are in the table in the next section.


### **1. Registrations by Channel**


Registrations by channel show which campaigns actually fill seats. Add UTM parameters to every registration link (email, LinkedIn, paid ads, partners) so each sign-up carries its source. Google’s guide to


**[collecting campaign data with custom URLs](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/10917952)** explains the naming rules. Our


**[Event Registration](https://inevent.com/en/registration-forms-rsvp-invites.php)** tool saves that source on each attendee profile, so you can sort sign-ups by channel at any time.


### ****


### **2. Registration Conversion Rate**


Registration conversion rate tells you how well your event page turns visitors into registrants. A low rate with high traffic usually points to the page itself: a long form, an unclear agenda, or a hidden price. Test one change at a time, such as removing optional form fields.


### **3. Cost per Registration**


Cost per registration shows what each sign-up costs, channel by channel. Compare channels before you shift budget. A channel with fewer registrations can still win if each sign-up is cheaper and later converts to pipeline.


### **4. Email Open Rate and Click-Through Rate**


Email is still the main invite channel for most events, so track email open rate and click-through rate for every invite and reminder. Opens show subject-line pull. Clicks show whether the content made people act. Compare each send with your own past events rather than generic benchmarks.


### **5. Attendance Rate and No-Show Rate**


The attendance rate compares check-ins with registrations, and no-show rate is the gap between them. A rising no-show rate usually means reminders went out too early or too rarely. With


**[Badge Printing & Check-In](https://inevent.com/en/live-badge-printing-accreditation-software.php)** , every badge scan updates the count live, so you see the attendance rate while doors are still open.


### **6. Session Attendance and Attendee Engagement**


Session scans, poll responses, Q&A questions, and app activity show attendee engagement in real time. For hybrid events, count remote viewers who join through virtual and hybrid streaming alongside in-room scans, so both audiences show up in the numbers. Meetings booked through AI matchmaking are a strong engagement signal too, because they show attendees found people worth meeting.


### **7. Social Reach and Branded Hashtag Use**


Social metrics show how far the event traveled beyond the room. Track reach, impressions, mentions of your branded hashtag, and click-through rate on event posts. Click-through rate is clicks divided by impressions, not the other way around.


***Team Tip:*** *Create one registration link per channel before launch and lock your UTM naming convention: utm_source=linkedin, never “LinkedIn” or “li”. Mixed spellings split one channel into three rows in your reports, and you can’t fix it once registrations start coming in. Keep the convention in a shared sheet that every agency and partner uses.*


#### **8. Net Promoter Score (NPS)**


Net Promoter Score measures how likely attendees are to recommend your event. Send a post-event survey within 24 hours with one question on a 0–10 scale. Scores of 9–10 are promoters, 7–8 are passives, and 0–6 are detractors. Add one open question, such as “What should we change next time?” because those answers often explain


**[how successful your event really was](https://inevent.com/blog/events/how-to-measure-event-success.html)** better than the score alone. HubSpot’s walkthrough on


**[how to calculate NPS](https://blog.hubspot.com/service/how-to-calculate-nps)** covers the method step by step.


### **9. Leads and Marketing Qualified Leads**


Count every lead captured at booths, sessions, and meetings, then track how many become marketing qualified leads. Lead generation volume alone can flatter an event. The MQL rate shows whether you attracted the right people.


### **10. Pipeline Influenced and Revenue**


Pipeline influenced is the total value of sales opportunities tied to contacts who attended, usually within 90 days. A CRM integration makes this possible: event data syncs into each contact record, so sales can follow up and marketing can report the result.[Finario, a capital-planning software company](https://inevent.com/en/finario-successful-video-marketing-strategies.php) , runs this as a two-way flow with our Salesforce integration. Webinar registrants land in Salesforce as new leads automatically, session-level lead scoring shows sales who engaged most, and existing pipeline contacts are pulled back into upcoming event invitations.


### **11. Cost per Attendee**


Cost per attendee divides total event cost by the people who actually attended, not the people who registered. Using check-ins keeps the number honest when no-shows are high.


### **12. Event Marketing ROI**


Event marketing ROI compares the revenue an event influenced with what it cost. ROI is the KPI leadership asks about first and the one most teams calculate wrong; the formula and a worked example follow below.


##


**Event Marketing KPI Formulas With Worked Examples**


The examples below use one sample event: 8,000 landing page visitors, 600 registrations, 420 check-ins, $84,000 total cost, and $210,000 in attributed revenue.


KPI Formula Worked example


**Registration conversion rate** Registrations ÷ landing page visitors × 100 600 ÷ 8,000 × 100 = 7.5%


**Cost per registration** Channel spend ÷ registrations from that channel $3,000 ÷ 150 LinkedIn sign-ups = $20


**Email click-through rate** Clicks ÷ emails delivered × 100 900 ÷ 20,000 × 100 = 4.5%


**Attendance rate** Check-ins ÷ registrations × 100 420 ÷ 600 × 100 = 70%


**No-show rate** 100% − attendance rate 100% − 70% = 30%


If you prefer a ratio, divide attributed revenue by total cost. A result above 1 means the event earned back more than it spent, and exactly 1 is break-even.


### **How Do You Calculate Event Marketing ROI?**


Calculate event marketing ROI by subtracting total event cost from the revenue the event influenced, then dividing by total cost and multiplying by 100. An event that cost $84,000 and influenced $210,000 in closed revenue returns 150%. Any result above 0% means the event earned back more than it cost.


The hard part is attribution, not the math. Nielsen’s 2025


**[Marketing ROI Blueprint](https://www.nielsen.com/news-center/2025/nielsen-unveils-makerting-roi-blueprint/)** found that 85% of marketers feel confident measuring ROI, yet only 32% measure it holistically across traditional and digital channels. Events often fall into that gap, because registrations, badge scans, and closed deals live in different tools. Agree with sales before the event on the attribution window (60 or 90 days) and which touch count. Once that’s settled, you can break the return down by ticket sales, sponsorships, and new deals, the same way teams


**[measure their event return on investment](https://inevent.com/blog/tech-and-trends/measuring-your-event-return-on-investment.html)** across a full event program.


### **How Do You Track Event Marketing Performance?**


Track event marketing performance by connecting three data sources: tagged registration links, live check-in and engagement data, and your CRM. Event marketing analytics then shows each attendee’s journey from first click to closed deal in one report, so you can compare channels, events, and formats without merging spreadsheets by hand.


Here’s the setup, InEvent event strategists use with marketing teams:


- **Tag every link.** Campaign attribution starts with consistent UTM parameters on every invite, ad, and partner post.


- **Capture the source at registration.** Store the channel on the attendee profile, not in a separate spreadsheet.


- **Scan everything on-site.** Badge scans at entry, sessions, and booths turn attendance into data.


- **Sync to your CRM daily.** Sales sees event activity on each contact while the lead is still warm.


- **Review one dashboard.** Our


**[Marketing Manager](https://inevent.com/en/marketing-branding-event-trends-roi.php)** solution puts registrations, engagement, and pipeline in one event analytics dashboard.


- **Report at 30, 60, and 90 days.** B2B deals often close after the event, so the first report is never the final one.

##


**Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What are the 5 key KPIs for an event?**


The five KPIs most event teams track are registrations, attendance rate, attendee engagement, net promoter score, and ROI. Together, they cover demand, turnout, experience, satisfaction, and business return. Add pipeline influenced for B2B events and social reach for brand events, but keep each event to five KPIs so every number has an owner.


### **What is a good NPS for an event?**


A good event NPS is any score above 0, because it means promoters outnumber detractors. Many teams treat 30 or higher as strong and 50 or higher as excellent. Compare against your own past events of the same format, since conferences, webinars, and customer summits naturally score differently.


### **What is a good event attendance rate?**


A good attendance rate depends on price and format. Paid in-person events usually keep more registrants than free events or webinars, where no-shows run higher. Set your benchmark from your last three events of the same type, then improve it with reminders at seven days, one day, and two hours before start.


### **How often should you track event marketing KPIs?**


Track event marketing KPIs weekly from launch, then daily in the final two weeks before the event. Watch attendance and engagement live on event day. After the event, review leads within 48 hours, and report pipeline and ROI at 30, 60, and 90 days because B2B deals often close well after the event.


### **What is the difference between event KPIs and event marketing KPIs?**


Event KPIs judge the whole event, including logistics, budget, and attendee satisfaction. Event marketing KPIs focus on promotion and business impact: which channels drove registrations, what each attendee cost, and how much pipeline followed. Most teams track both, with marketing owning the second group and reporting it alongside sales.


##
